doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Steely Dan and L.A. session life
title: The Deacon Blues voicing and Christlieb's solo
summary: He explains turning an E minor chord into a G13 voicing and how Pete's solo forced one rewrite.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah Plas of course. So it was supposed to be, I think we did it, we had four sessions, evening sessions planned to do all — was it eight tunes? Seven tunes? Eight tunes? I’m not sure. And I had written you know, they had given me their master rhythm parts which the rhythm section had used to make their tracks. And if I may get technical for a second, the tune “Deacon Blues” started out with a chord which was just a triad. It was a E minor, you could call it an E minor chord with a G in the bass. G in the bottom E and B. That’s what the rhythm section played, the very first chord. Now that chord kept coming up later at the point where I was supposed to come in with horns. So you know I’ve got all these horns, I’m not just going to play three notes. That would be ridiculous. So I pulled what I used to refer to as an Oliver Nelson because Oliver was my hero, my mentor. And he loved those very close juicy voicings where the juicy notes, you know the extended parts of the chord are not up here but they’re right in the middle. So I took that first chord, that E minor G bass, and turned it into a G 13 chord. So it was G on the bottom and then E, the E below middle C, and then F – A – B – and E on top. So it’s like a G 13. With the E part, the 13th part in octaves.
Was it a, speaking of being technical, was it a C sharp or was it a C?
There was no C in it at all, it was a G chord.
Oh it was a G chord. Okay.
G – E – F – A – B – E.

Right? So that’s and it kind of went on that way with this tight voicings. And I didn’t know, man, I had no idea how they would react but they liked it. And in fact with the exception of one tune, and that was “Deacon Blues” everything went as written. Talk about good fortune smiling on Tom. But the only tune that I had to change was a tune in which they had inserted something after they gave me these tapes, and the thing they had inserted was Pete Christlieb’s solo on “Deacon Blues.” I had written something else in there and I had to re-do that and make I guess a background or I forget what I did. But in any case Pete’s solo on “Deacon Blues” was just monumental.
